quarterly_data.signal: CFO Brice Hill detailed the leading indicators behind the demand call. Applied runs a fab tracker of well over 100 factories announced across the world, with more than 10 added in each of the last two quarters, and the rolling eight-quarter forecast from its largest customers has risen every single quarter this year. Looking one level further out, cloud service provider capex forecasts have risen all year - over $700 billion this year for the U.S. companies and almost $1 trillion for the global companies. Management says the medium-term ramp is gated by clean room, and there is more demand than there is supply.
quarterly_data.figure: fab tracker well over 100 factories, more than 10 added in each of the last two quarters; CSP capex over $700 billion this year for U.S. companies, almost $1 trillion globally

quarterly_data.signal: Capacity and supply-chain readiness: Applied has invested and is investing so that it can produce double the amount of systems each quarter that it is producing today - a capacity statement, not a revenue forecast. Clean room typically takes two, three or four years to put in place. Applied aggregates the eight-quarter customer forecasts by component type and sends them to its suppliers - typically referenced as 2,000 plus suppliers - so they get 8-quarter advance notice to add capacity, and that forecast has risen every single quarter this year.
quarterly_data.figure: capacity to produce double the amount of systems each quarter; 2,000 plus suppliers on 8-quarter forecast; clean room takes two, three or four years

quarterly_data.signal: CFO gave the prior-year base for advanced packaging for the first time: it was a $1.4 billion business for Applied Materials last year and is growing more than 70% this year, and management expects advanced packaging to grow apace with leading-edge logic and DRAM going forward. On panels, the industry is currently in development - Applied has revenue on its panel processing equipment but management does not think there is any volume production at this point - and the open engineering issues are thermals on a panel substrate and form factor, with some companies experimenting at wafer size and some larger. Applied is leaning on its display experience, has invested in lithography capabilities, and has eBeam products to inspect panels and other package types. Recent tuck-ins: NEX for fine line interconnects on panel levels and an X-ray technology company to inspect micro-bumps between stacked chips.
quarterly_data.figure: advanced packaging $1.4 billion last year, growing more than 70% this year

quarterly_data.signal: DRAM is shifting from line upgrades to greenfield, which changes the equipment intensity. About 1.6 million DRAM wafers per month was the right number a year ago; this year the industry is adding 400,000 more wafer starts per month of capacity, and Applied sees 300,000 to 400,000 additional wafer starts a month of new DRAM capacity for the next several years, taking the industry from 1.6 million to 2 million to 2.4 million wafer starts per month. Economics: an upgrade factory takes about 25% of the equipment investment of a greenfield, where process equipment is more like $10 billion for 100,000 wafer starts of capacity.
quarterly_data.figure: about 1.6 million DRAM wafers per month a year ago; 400,000 more wafer starts per month added this year; 300,000 to 400,000 additional wafer starts a month for the next several years; upgrade about 25% of the equipment investment; greenfield process equipment more like $10 billion for 100,000 wafer starts

quarterly_data.signal: On HBM de-speccing: when customers lower the number of stacked High-Bandwidth Memory in a system they are doing it to get more system output and ship more AI data center systems in total against the memory constraint, which means shipping more GPUs, more CPUs and more accelerators per memory chip. Applied views the effect on equipment demand as overall neutral and says it has not seen a reduction in demand in the business because of this phenomenon.

NAND bit demand is very strong - management puts it in probably the high 20% range - but adding layers is so productive in bits per square centimeter that fewer wafers are needed to meet that demand. The result is an upgrade cycle rather than new factories: fewer greenfield fabs, no growth in wafer starts, and a smaller equipment market, which Applied expects to continue for at least the next few years. Wafer starts for NAND are declining on a yearly basis even though bit growth is the same as DRAM.
quarterly_data.figure: NAND bit demand probably in the high 20% range; upgrade cycle makes the equipment market smaller for at least the next few years
